name: Download Speed
description: Find the maximum data transfer rate from computer 1 to computer n through a network of directed connections with given capacities.
why_hard: The canonical from-scratch max flow implementation exercise (Edmonds-Karp/Dinic) with no modeling trick to hide behind.

name: Distinct Routes
description: Find the maximum number of edge-disjoint paths from room 1 to room n in a directed graph and output the paths themselves.
why_hard: Requires not just the max-flow value but decomposing the resulting flow into explicit paths, a step many implementations skip.

name: Fox and Dinner
description: Seat foxes at round tables (each with at least 3 foxes) so that the ages of any two adjacent foxes sum to a prime.
why_hard: The flow network isn't given — you must notice primes > 2 force even/odd parity pairing, turning the seating constraint into a bipartite degree-exactly-2 flow model.

name: Delivery Bears
description: Split a required flow between two bear species along edge capacities in a fixed ratio while maximizing total flow.
why_hard: Combines binary search on the answer with a max-flow feasibility check under a ratio constraint on edge usage.

name: Police Chase
description: Find the minimum number of edges to remove to disconnect node 1 from node n, and report which edges to cut.
why_hard: Direct application of max-flow min-cut duality, including reconstructing the actual cut edges from the residual graph.

name: Petya and Graph
description: Choose a subgraph maximizing (sum of edge weights) minus (sum of weights of vertices touched by chosen edges).
why_hard: A non-obvious instance of the maximum-weight closure / project-selection problem, solved by reducing to min cut via source/sink edges on vertices and edges.

name: Rectangle Painting 2
description: Paint possibly-overlapping rectangles in two colors to minimize the total mismatched-color area in their pairwise overlaps.
why_hard: Requires recognizing a 2-coloring cost-minimization structure as a project-selection/min-cut instance over interacting overlap regions.

name: School Dance
description: Find the maximum matching between boys and girls given a list of pairs willing to dance together.
why_hard: The baseline Kuhn's algorithm / Hopcroft-Karp implementation problem, with input sizes that punish naive O(VE) blow-ups.

name: Exploration Plan
description: Find the minimum time limit so that N teams starting in various cities can collectively occupy at least K distinct cities.
why_hard: Layers all-pairs shortest paths and binary search on top of a bipartite matching feasibility check (Hall's theorem), a common competitive pattern.

name: Round Marriage
description: Match bridegrooms to brides placed around a circle to minimize the maximum walking distance any bride must travel.
why_hard: The circular structure and min-max objective require binary search combined with a Hall's-theorem-based matching existence check, not a direct matching computation.

name: Anti-Palindromize
description: Rearrange a string into an antipalindromic permutation maximizing the sum of "beauty" values at positions that keep their original character.
why_hard: Classic MCMF assignment: build a flow network pairing symmetric position-pairs to letter-pairs with costs, a staple "recognize the assignment structure" exercise.

name: Red-Blue Graph
description: Color bipartite-graph edges red/blue (or leave uncolored) at a cost to satisfy per-vertex majority-color constraints, minimizing total cost.
why_hard: Non-obvious reduction of a combinatorial coloring/degree-constraint problem into an MCMF instance; frequently cited in curated "MCMF example" lists.

name: Build String
description: Build a target string t by deleting characters from n source strings, each character removed from string s_i costing i rubles and capped at a_i total removals, minimizing total cost.
why_hard: A clean "characters = flow units, costs = per-source-string price, capacities = per-string budget" MCMF formulation.

name: Four Melodies
description: Select four disjoint, non-intersecting "melody" subsequences (each with the arithmetic/mod-7 melody property) from a note sequence to maximize total length.
why_hard: Harder generalization of the well-known "Two Melodies" problem; needs a carefully constructed layered MCMF graph with node-splitting to bound the number of selected sequences.

name: MCF
description: Find the minimum-cost circulation in a DAG-like flow network subject to the extra constraint that each edge's flow must match its capacity's parity.
why_hard: Explicitly named "MCF" by the setters; forces adapting standard min-cost-flow machinery to handle parity constraints on edge flows.

name: Task Assignment
description: Given n employees, n tasks, and a full cost matrix, assign every employee exactly one task minimizing total cost (and output the assignment).
why_hard: This is the canonical, textbook statement of the assignment problem — the direct target of the Hungarian algorithm (confirmed as the flagship "assignment" practice problem in USACO Guide's Min-Cost-Flow module).

name: Chef Monocarp
description: Assign each of n dishes to a distinct positive-integer removal time T, minimizing the sum of |T - t_i| over all dishes.
why_hard: Structurally a full bipartite min-cost perfect matching (dishes × time slots); the intended O(n log n) solution exploits the 1-D cost structure, but it is a genuine, frequently-cited real-world instance of the assignment problem.

name: Vasya and Endless Credits
description: Choose an order to activate n credit offers (one per month) to maximize the money available at some point before repayments catch up.
why_hard: Listed by USACO Guide as a direct application of the assignment-problem/Hungarian-algorithm machinery (offers × activation-month slots with a cost/profit matrix).

name: T-shirts Distribution
description: Given fixed stock counts for six t-shirt sizes and n participants who each want either one fixed size or either of two neighboring sizes, decide if everyone can be given a shirt and construct a valid assignment.
why_hard: The six sizes form a tiny path graph where flexible requests are edges between neighbors; satisfying a flexible participant can starve a rigid neighbor, so the fix is an augmenting-path (max-flow) adjustment cascading along the size chain rather than one-pass greedy assignment.

name: Single-use Stones
description: Given a river of width w crossable by jumps of length up to l and a limited supply of stones at each intermediate distance (each stone usable by only one frog), find the maximum number of frogs that can cross.
why_hard: Scarce, single-use stones are modeled as flow capacity via node-splitting (in/out per position) with edges to every position within jump range; the trick is realizing frog crossings are literally units of flow rather than a shortest-path or simulation problem.

name: Valuable Paper
description: Given n factories and n airports connected by weighted roads, find a perfect one-to-one matching between them minimizing the maximum road weight used, or report it's impossible.
why_hard: The min-max objective needs binary search over edge weights, and each check is a genuine perfect bipartite matching existence test on the threshold subgraph — practice recognizing when a direct Kuhn's/Hopcroft-Karp call is the right feasibility check, not Hall's-theorem counting.

name: Koxia and Game
description: Count arrays c (mod a prime) such that, in the round game where Koxia removes one of {a_i, b_i, c_i} each round and adversarial Mahiru then picks the surviving value, Koxia can always force the final sequence to be a permutation of 1..n.
why_hard: Turning "Koxia can force a permutation regardless of Mahiru's pick" into a checkable condition reduces to a Hall's-theorem-style deficiency/matching argument over the value graph formed by a and b, then the count of valid c must respect that structural condition rather than being a plain combinatorial count.
